title: 1 Chronicles 1:28–54
context: From Abraham the list names Isaac and Ishmael, then Ishmael’s sons, then the sons of Keturah, whom this chapter calls Abraham’s concubine, then Isaac’s sons Esau and Israel, then Esau’s descendants, the sons of Seir, the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel, and the chiefs of Edom. The chief parallels are Genesis 25, for Ishmael and Keturah, and Genesis 36, for Esau, Seir, and Edom’s kings and chiefs. The Chronicler often shortens those chapters and sometimes differs in spelling or arrangement; the differences should be named, not harmonized. Keturah is “Abraham’s concubine” here, while Genesis 25:1 introduces her as a wife. Timna is listed among the sons of Eliphaz in 1:36, whereas Genesis 36:12 describes Timna as Eliphaz’s concubine and the mother of Amalek. Other names also differ in spelling from Genesis 36, and those differences are named rather than resolved. Site identifications for the Edomite cities should remain modest. Both traditions read the unit as Israel’s brother-peoples set in place before the book turns, in chapter 2, to the sons of Israel and to Judah’s royal line.

verses.text: The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael.” The two are named together, as they later bury Abraham in Genesis 25:9, before the list treats each line. Israel’s ancestor is not isolated from his brother.

Arminian readers hear a real household: both sons belong to Abraham, and both will be traced, though not to the same later role.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from this pairing. Genesis 25 will be the chief parallel for the next verses; here the Chronicler simply names the two sons.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: These are their generations: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,
verses.arminianNotes:
Ishmael’s generations begin with “the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth; then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,” matching the order of Genesis 25:13, which that chapter also marks as birth order.

Arminian readers take the names as a genuine record of Ishmael’s house, a related family, not a foil to be dismissed or allegorized.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same opening as Genesis 25:13, now in the Chronicler’s shorter style, still placing Abraham’s firstborn son’s line on the page.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema,
verses.arminianNotes:
The Ishmaelite list continues: “Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema,” as in Genesis 25:14–15, where Mishma, Dumah, and Massa stand in one verse and Hadad and Tema in the next.

Arminian readers keep the five names as history, without guessing certain desert sites for each.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the parallel across Genesis 25:14–15 and decline to force identifications the verse does not make.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael.
verses.arminianNotes:
The list closes: “Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael.” The three names and the summary match Genesis 25:15–16, without that chapter’s notice of twelve princes, villages, and years.

Arminian readers receive the summary as a complete naming of Ishmael’s sons, then the Chronicler will turn to Keturah.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a shortened form of Genesis 25:15–16. The sons are named; the wider comment of Genesis is left aside here.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Keturah, Abraham’s concubine: she bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan.
verses.arminianNotes:
Keturah is called “Abraham’s concubine” and her sons are Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah, with Sheba and Dedan under Jokshan. Genesis 25:1–3 has the same sons, and there Keturah is introduced as a wife. The difference of title should be named, not erased. Chronicles does not list Dedan’s further sons from Genesis 25:3.

Arminian readers can hold both notices without choosing one as the only true description.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report the parallel and the different description of Keturah, without a forced harmony. The names of the sons agree.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Midian’s sons are Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah, “All these were the sons of Keturah.” The five names and the closing formula match Genesis 25:4.

Arminian readers take Midian’s house as a real related people, later familiar in Israel’s story, here simply catalogued.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same close as Genesis 25:4. Keturah’s descendants have been named; the list will now return to Isaac.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Abraham became the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Abraham became the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.” After Ishmael and Keturah, the Chronicler restates Isaac and then names his two sons, using Israel rather than Jacob.

Arminian readers hear a deliberate turn to the chosen line’s next generation, still with Esau named beside Israel, as in Genesis.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same hinge. Genesis 25 and 36 will now be the parallels for Esau; chapter 2 will take up Israel’s sons.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.” The five names match the sons given in Genesis 36:4–5, 10, and 14, though Genesis there also names their mothers. This verse does not.

Arminian readers receive Esau’s sons as a real family record, parallel to Genesis 36 and not to be turned into types of later enmity alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the parallel in view and note what is omitted. The five sons stand, as in Genesis, at the head of Edom’s houses.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, Timna, and Amalek.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphaz’s sons are Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, Timna, and Amalek. Genesis 36:11 has Zepho, not Zephi, and Genesis 36:12 presents Timna as Eliphaz’s concubine and the mother of Amalek, not as one of the sons in the same list. The spelling and the arrangement differ and should not be forced together.

Arminian readers name those differences and still read a genuine Edomite genealogy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise leave Zephi/Zepho and Timna’s placement as differences between 1:36 and Genesis 36:11–12, without a required harmony.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.” The four names match Genesis 36:13 exactly in WEB spelling.

Arminian readers take the verse as a straightforward parallel, a quiet agreement of the two lists at this point.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the close match with Genesis 36:13. Not every line in this chapter differs from its parallel.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.” Genesis 36:20–21 names the same seven as the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land. Chronicles does not here call them Horites, as Genesis does.

Arminian readers still treat them as the prior inhabitants already honored in the Genesis 36 notes, named because they were truly there.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same seven names as Genesis 36:20–21, in shorter form, the people of Seir placed beside Esau’s house.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Lotan: Hori and Homam; and Timna was Lotan’s sister.
verses.arminianNotes:
Lotan’s sons are Hori and Homam, “and Timna was Lotan’s sister.” Genesis 36:22 has Hori and Heman, and also says that Lotan’s sister was Timna. Homam and Heman differ; the notice about Timna agrees.

Arminian readers report the spelling difference neutrally and do not build a story on it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave Homam and Heman as a difference from Genesis 36:22, while the kinship note about Timna is the same.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Shobal: Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shobal’s sons are Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam; Zibeon’s are Aiah and Anah. Genesis 36:23–24 has Alvan and Shepho where this verse has Alian and Shephi, and the same two sons of Zibeon. Genesis also tells of Anah and the hot springs; Chronicles does not.

Arminian readers name the variants and the omitted story, without forcing a single spelling.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep Alian/Alvan and Shephi/Shepho as differences, and they do not supply Genesis 36:24’s narrative here.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The son of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hamran, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The son of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hamran, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.” Genesis 36:25 names Dishon and Oholibamah as Anah’s children; this verse names only Dishon. Genesis 36:26 has Hemdan where this verse has Hamran. The lists are close, not identical.

Arminian readers let those differences stand, as in the rest of this Edom section.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse a forced harmony of Hamran and Hemdan, or of the children of Anah. The parallel is Genesis 36:25–26.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezer’s sons are Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan; Dishan’s are Uz and Aran. Genesis 36:27–28 has Akan, not Jaakan, and the other four names the same.

Arminian readers note Jaakan and Akan as a spelling difference and do not allegorize Uz or the rest.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave that variant beside the otherwise matching lists of Genesis 36:27–28.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Now these are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel: Bela the son of Beor; and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Edomite kings begin: “these are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel: Bela the son of Beor; and the name of his city was Dinhabah.” The heading and the first king match Genesis 36:31–32 closely.

Arminian readers take the notice as a real historical sequence in Edom, earlier than Israel’s own kingship, not as a slight against Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same heading as Genesis 36:31–32. The Chronicler records Edom’s kings as part of the world’s families around Israel.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.” The succession matches Genesis 36:33. Bozrah is named as Jobab’s place; further site claims should remain modest.

Arminian readers read a straightforward royal succession, parallel to Genesis, without turning the death-and-reign formula into a type.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the verse as the same step as Genesis 36:33, one king following another in Edom.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.” The wording matches Genesis 36:34. The Temanite land is given as Husham’s origin, not as a fully mapped territory here.

Arminian readers keep the succession as history, a second change of reign in the Edomite list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same parallel in Genesis 36:34 and decline to press the geography beyond what is said.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who struck Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his place; and the name of his city was Avith.
verses.arminianNotes:
Husham dies, and Hadad son of Bedad, “who struck Midian in the field of Moab,” reigns; his city is Avith. Genesis 36:35 has the same deed and the same city. The campaign is named, not described at length.

Arminian readers take the notice as a brief historical note already present in Genesis, not as a cue for typology.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report the parallel. The two lists agree here on Hadad, Midian, Moab, and Avith.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.” The verse matches Genesis 36:36. Masrekah is named; it should not be identified more closely than the text allows.

Arminian readers hear another plain succession, the formula unchanged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take it as the same step as Genesis 36:36, still the kings of Edom before Israel’s kingship.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth by the River reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth by the River reigned in his place.” Genesis 36:37 has the same succession; WEB there has “the river” in lowercase. The river is not further named, and guesses should be modest.

Arminian readers leave the place as the verse states it and do not build a map on an uncertain identification.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the parallel and the reserved geography. The king is Shaul of Rehoboth by the River, as both lists say.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Shaul died, and Baal Hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Shaul died, and Baal Hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.” The wording matches Genesis 36:38. The name Baal Hanan is given without comment or allegory.

Arminian readers take the succession as another historical link in the Edomite reigns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same verse as Genesis 36:38, a simple change of king, still in the chronicler’s catalogue of Edom.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Baal Hanan died, and Hadad reigned in his place; and the name of his city was Pai. His wife’s name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab.
verses.arminianNotes:
Baal Hanan dies, and Hadad reigns; his city is Pai, and his wife is Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab. Genesis 36:39 has Hadar, not Hadad, and Pau, not Pai, with the same wife’s ancestry. The name and city differ; the family notice agrees.

Arminian readers name Hadad/Hadar and Pai/Pau as differences and do not force a single form.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise leave those spellings as they stand in the two lists, Genesis 36:39 and this verse, without a required explanation.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: Then Hadad died. The chiefs of Edom were: chief Timna, chief Aliah, chief Jetheth,
verses.arminianNotes:
Hadad dies, and the chiefs of Edom begin: chief Timna, chief Aliah, chief Jetheth. Genesis 36:40 has chief Alvah, not Aliah, with Timna and Jetheth the same. The heading in Genesis also explains the chiefs by families and places; this verse is shorter.

Arminian readers report Aliah and Alvah as a spelling difference and keep the list as a record of chiefs, not as a coded roster.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to harmonize Aliah and Alvah. The parallel is the chief-list of Genesis 36:40–43, begun here.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon,
verses.arminianNotes:
The chiefs continue: “chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon,” matching Genesis 36:41 in WEB spelling.

Arminian readers take the three as a straightforward continuation of the Edomite chief-list, in agreement with Genesis at this point.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the close match with Genesis 36:41. The catalogue of chiefs is still underway.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar,
verses.arminianNotes:
Next are “chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar,” the same three, in the same order, as Genesis 36:42.

Arminian readers keep the names as historical chiefs of Edom, without turning Kenaz or Teman into symbols here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same step as Genesis 36:42, a continuing parallel in the closing list of the chapter.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.

verses.text: chief Magdiel, and chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom.
verses.arminianNotes:
The unit ends: “chief Magdiel, and chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom.” The last two names and the summary match the close of Genesis 36:43, without that verse’s longer close about habitations and Esau the father of the Edomites.

Arminian readers take this as the Chronicler’s ending of the world-family section, before Israel’s own sons in chapter 2.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a shortened close of Genesis 36:43. Edom’s chiefs are named; the book is ready to turn to the sons of Israel and, in time, to the royal line.

Both traditions take the Chronicler still to be placing Israel among related families, here Abraham’s other sons and Esau’s house, without allegory and without forcing the Genesis lists into one spelling.
